name: Log: Year Eight
author: Withheld (A-tier, GLMZ Narrows circuit)
description: A personal log written at the close of an unnamed freelancer's eighth year of active work. The author reached A-tier ranking sometime in year six and has remained there. The document was found archived in a dead drop exchange in the Narrows West district, flagged by a broker as a 'calibration read' — recommended reading for B-tier workers approaching advancement. The author has not been identified. The log does not appear to be intended for distribution; its presence in the exchange suggests someone thought it should be passed on.
body:
Year Eight. Writing this because I said I would, back at year one, back at year three, back at year six. I don't know if those logs still exist. The apartment I kept them in doesn't.

The body first, because that's what people ask about, and it's the most countable thing.

Left arm is full prosthetic from the mid-humerus. That happened year four — the Portage job, structural collapse, not combat, which is embarrassing in the way that only matters to people who've never actually been in a structural collapse. The first replacement was a Yuen Dynamics Series 7, which I bought used and which gave me chronic phantom pain in the missing fingers for fourteen months. Traded up to a Helix Mech third-gen when I had a good quarter, and the phantom pain stopped about sixty percent. It's still there in cold weather. I don't mention this to clients.

Right knee has a ceramic-composite patella replacement and partial ACL reconstruction, done in year two after a drop that I landed badly. This was before I had augment debt so I went through the Narrows clinic, which means it was done competently but without the follow-up care. The knee tells me when it's going to rain. This is occasionally useful.

Chronic tinnitus, left ear, since year three. The source is contested — could be the IED-adjacent incident in the Shelf 9 sweep, could be accumulated. Either way it's constant. I have learned to work around it. I can still hear. I mention it here because it never made it into any formal medical record, and because forgetting to list it would be the kind of self-deception I'm trying to avoid.

Two cracked ribs, healed incorrectly, year five. They ache when I twist too fast. I have adapted my movement accordingly.

The neural overlay — second-generation Lattice, installed year two — is intact. It has had one partial rebuild after a close-range scrambler hit and I have since developed a persistent low-level processing delay in spatial mapping that is within tolerance but that I notice. I notice it most in enclosed spaces with multiple moving targets. I have adjusted. This adjustment may someday be insufficient.

That's the body.

Money is harder to explain to people who don't do this work, because the numbers sound large until you actually itemize them.

I've had three good years out of eight. Good meaning net positive after expenses — medical, equipment, transport, broker cuts, dead drop maintenance, the informal costs of keeping vouches warm. Two of those years were actually good, meaning I felt solvent. One was good on paper and I spent the surplus clearing the debt from year six, which was the bad year. Year six was the bad year because I turned down three jobs based on intel that turned out to be wrong and I took a fourth job based on intel that also turned out to be wrong, and the net result was four months of very little income and one month of active medical debt accumulation.

Current state: not in debt. Have a reserve. The reserve is the largest I've ever held, which is Φ 14,200, which sounds like something until I consider that my last augment-related medical bill was Φ 11,000 and came with no warning. So the reserve is a margin, not security. I know the difference now. I did not know it in year one.

Who is still here.

My sister. She's in the Canopy — different tier, different world, she married into corporate adjacency and I have never once asked her for money and she has never once asked me what I do specifically. We talk on her schedule. It's not close but it's real.

Varo. He's been my broker for six years and I trust him to the extent I trust anyone in this work, which means I verify things he tells me and he knows I verify them and neither of us pretends otherwise. He has sent me work when I was near broke without making it charity, which is a skill I respect.

Keel. She's a medic, works the Narrows clinic Tuesdays and black market Thursdays. We are not together in any formal sense. We have dinner sometimes. She has kept me alive twice, once professionally and once personally, and I don't have a cleaner way to say that.

The people who are not here are longer to list. I won't. The ones who died in the work are mourned specifically and in private. The ones who left because of what the work does to a person — I understand that. Year three was when most of those departures happened. You either find people who can live adjacent to this or you lose them. I mostly lost them.

What I'm good at now that I wasn't in year one: patience. Reading rooms. Knowing when a client is lying versus when they're just uninformed — different problems, different responses. I'm good at refusal. I wasn't. I used to take anything because the fear of empty weeks was constant and total. Now I can hold a week, hold two weeks, because I understand that the wrong job costs more than the lost income.

What I still take because I have to: I take work I find distasteful if the alternative is the reserve dropping below a functional threshold. I have a number in my head — the floor — and below that floor I take what I'm offered within certain limits. Those limits are mine and I won't list them here. But the floor work exists. Anyone who tells you it doesn't, at their level, is either lying or wealthy enough that their floor has never been tested. I've done jobs in the last eight years that I don't regret exactly but that I hold differently than the others. I know what I did. That's the most honest thing I can say.

Would I do it again.

Not the question I asked at year three, which was whether I should stop. I should have stopped at year three in the sense that three years in was when the cost was visible but before it was fully paid. A clean exit was still possible then. I don't think it's clean anymore. I don't mean that dramatically — I mean that I've been doing this long enough that I don't know what a different life would use me for. The specific skills I have, the way I read situations now, the tolerance I've built for sustained uncertainty — those don't translate cleanly to anything with a paycheck and a supervisor. Maybe they do and I've just convinced myself they don't because the alternative requires something I'm not ready to do.

There are days I am exactly who I want to be and I'm doing exactly what I'm capable of and it means something real — someone got out of something they shouldn't have been in, or something got stopped that should have been stopped. Those days exist.

There are days I'm just a contractor who did a job and got paid and I couldn't tell you the outcome because I was paid not to track it.

Year nine starts whenever I wake up from a full night's sleep, which has been inconsistent. I am going to try to sleep. I'm going to try to hold the reserve above the floor. I'm going to try to be careful about the same things I have not been careful enough about for eight years.

I'd do it again. I think. I'm not sure that's the same as saying I should.
